overview: Amangu are among the Aboriginal peoples of Western Australia’s Mid West, including the Geraldton region. Amangu identity continues within wider Southern Yamatji and Yamatji relationships. Archaeology, place-based knowledge and living artists illuminate this history without reducing its communities to the boundaries of an imported map.

periods.title: Pastoral expansion and altered access to Country
periods.summary: Colonial stock routes and settlement appropriated Aboriginal pathways and water sources from the 1850s. The Old North Road assessment identifies disruption to Amangu, Yued and Whadjuk peoples whose lands the route crossed.

periods.title: Investigating Yellabidde Cave
periods.summary: Excavations begun in 2014, with Amangu Traditional Owners involved, documented a deep sequence of cave use. The 2016 research report extended the archaeological evidence for occupation of the northern coastal plain.

periods.title: Changing claims and continuing representation
periods.summary: The Wilunyu and Naaguja claims combined into the Southern Yamatji claim in 2017. YMAC reported that an elected Amangu working group continued to oversee earlier agreements and community development.

periods.title: A regional agreement and living community
periods.summary: The 2020 Yamatji Nation settlement combined a native title determination with an Indigenous Land Use Agreement. Amangu remain among the distinct identities represented in the region’s continuing community institutions.

sections.title: Cave finds and what they can tell us

items.text: At Yellabidde Cave, researchers recovered stone artifacts and charcoal from deposits extending back about 25,500 calibrated years before present. A younger charcoal fragment in a deep layer was judged intrusive. The sequence records intermittent occupation, not uninterrupted residence or proof that today’s named identities had identical boundaries throughout that span.

Quartz and limestone fragments at Yellabidde were interpreted as debris from making or modifying tools. Later layers also contained ochre and plant remains near hearths. Animal bones require another distinction: people, owls and mammalian predators all contributed to the deposit, so the whole bone collection cannot be read as a human menu.

Amangu Traditional Owners helped name the site Yellabidde after the emu eggshell found there. The cave had long been known locally before the 2014 archaeological excavation. Scientific investigation added dated evidence to a place already present in community knowledge; it did not discover an unknown landscape for its custodians.

sections.title: Food, water and connections between places

items.text: The city’s Yamaji heritage trail describes Champion Bay as a sheltered fishing ground used by people from across the Mid West. Nearby Chapman River offered camping places, while Greenough’s permanent waterholes supported wildlife and edible plants. These are connected regional examples, not evidence that only Amangu people used each location.

The Old North Road Stock Route followed a landscape already structured by Aboriginal pathways and water sources. Its heritage assessment records how colonial droving and settlement changed access to these places. Wells and road infrastructure therefore preserve a history of pastoral transport alongside the disruption of much older relationships with water and Country.

sections.title: Painting, performance and passing on knowledge

items.text: Nicole Dickerson’s Connection of Our People is an acrylic painting that links ancestors, stars, rivers and the ocean. The artist’s statement accompanies it in the Mid West Development Commission’s 2024 to 2025 report. Dickerson has Amangu, Naaguja, Wilunyu and Ngarluma connections; her individual work should not be treated as a generic design shared identically by all groups.

For Winthu Wangga in July 2024, Dickerson collaborated with poet Charmaine Papertalk Green on a drone-light and sound performance at Geraldton. Images and narration followed wind across inland and coastal Country. The production combined artistic knowledge with animation and sound design, creating a new medium for public storytelling.

Amangu performer Lucia Richardson appears in Star Dreaming, a 2021 film connecting a journey through radio astronomy with encounters with Yamaji artists. Its study guide records her explanation that painting, dancing and conversation pass knowledge between people. Her participation offers an example of young people contributing to cultural storytelling, rather than appearing only as its audience.

YMAC’s 2017 report traces changes from the Amangu claim to Wilunyu and then Southern Yamatji. It also states that earlier project agreements remained in force and that an elected Amangu working group continued making decisions about their implementation. Changes in a legal claim’s name therefore did not mean that Amangu identity had ceased.

The Yamatji Nation agreement names Amangu alongside other identities and explicitly recognizes continuing relationships with land and waters. It describes responsibilities guided by traditional laws and customs. This regional arrangement preserves distinctions among its constituent identities, rather than declaring that every group has one language or a single interchangeable history.

The Department of Justice dates the consent determination to 7 February 2020 and formal execution of the agreement to 24 February. It distinguishes recognized native title over particular parcels from the wider agreement and its benefits. A broad settlement area is not proof of exclusive title over every place inside it.

ending.text: Amangu people continue as part of the region’s living communities. Colonial land use disrupted access to Country, while later agreements and institutions address aspects of those losses. Amangu identity remains explicitly recognized within Yamatji Nation. The map’s 1878 cutoff marks the end of this imported coverage, not the people’s history.
